title: Mean contact depth gave no phase prediction gain in fixed linear models of 35 inputs to one leech neuron
abstract: We tested whether mean soma-to-contact path length improves phase prediction after contact count is known. The data link anatomy and voltage imaging from one leech ganglion. Each linear model excluded the complete activity record of the input it predicted. In 35 mapped inputs to motor neuron DE-3R, adding depth increased error by 4.77% in two swim trials and 5.66% in three left-bend trials. Count-preserving whole-input label tests gave right-tail p values of 0.5445 and 0.9255; both Holm values were 1.0. All planned descriptive variants also had negative gains. A later exact-moment audit gave reference mean gains of -3.95% and -4.09%, which explains why a negative gain alone does not show a biological depth effect. Independent tree paths, direct regression refits, exact synthetic assignments and a copied-source replay passed. One animal, selected inputs, uncertain matches, few trials, absent raw phase errors and a fixed linear model limit inference. The result does not show that contact depth has no computational role. Original code, aggregate evidence, figures, source hashes and external retrieval steps support reproduction. Source records and record-level derivatives remain outside the publication.

display.caption: Adding mean contact depth increased excluded-input prediction error in the tested fixed models. Histograms keep activity labels within exact contact counts. Negative gain means greater error after depth is added. The model checks are descriptive. The label draws do not describe differences across animals.
